objective: To spell words where the final consonant doubles before -ed or -er
defs: allowed to happen; given official permission
fully dedicated to something; carried out an action
liked one thing more than another
directed someone or something to another person or place

sentences.permitted: Mobile phones were not ____________________ inside the examination hall under any circumstances.
sentences.committed: The whole team was ____________________ to finishing the project before the end of term.
sentences.preferred: She ____________________ the seat by the window because she could watch the trains go by.
sentences.referred: The librarian ____________________ her to a book about local history that nobody else had ever borrowed.
sentences.occurred: It suddenly ____________________ to him that he had been solving the puzzle the wrong way round.
sentences.bigger: Manaus is far ____________________ than most people expect; it has a population of over two million.
sentences.thinner: The ice was much ____________________ at the edges of the lake, so they stayed near the centre.
sentences.sadder: There was no ____________________ ending in the whole book than the lighthouse keeper saying goodbye.
sentences.hotter: Brazil is significantly ____________________ than England for most of the year, with a tropical climate.
sentences.flatter: The south of England is much ____________________ than the north, with fewer hills and wider plains.

starter.question: Can you add -ed or -er to these words? What must you do first?
starter.ruleBox: Same doubling rule as -ing: short vowel + single consonant = double before -ed or -er. For two-syllable verbs, only double if the stress falls on the final syllable (per-MIT → permitted; EN-ter → entered, no double).

thisWeeksWordsQ: What do you notice about today's words?
thisWeeksWordsPrompt: Look at each base word. Why does the final consonant double before -ed or -er?
thisWeeksWordsExplanation: All today's words double the final consonant before -ed or -er. The rule is the same as for -ing: short vowel + single consonant = double. For two-syllable verbs, the stress must be on the final syllable: per-MIT → permitted (stress on -mit, so double). EN-ter → entered (stress on en-, so no double). The comparative adjectives big, thin, sad, hot and flat all follow the same short-vowel rule.

clicks.label: Base word
clicks.body: praeferre — to carry before or set in front

clicks.label: Original meaning
clicks.body: prae- (before) + ferre (to carry) — literally to carry something to the front.

clicks.label: Then
clicks.body: Came into English via Old French préférer, meaning to esteem one thing more highly than another.

clicks.label: Now
clicks.body: We use preferred to mean liked one option more than another.

clicks.label: In today's words
clicks.body: The stress falls on the final syllable (pre-FER), so the r doubles: prefer → preferred.

wordSortQ: Can you sort these words into two groups?

wordSort.box1sub: Long vowel, cluster, or stress on first syllable
wordSort.box2sub: Short vowel + single consonant (stress on final syllable for 2-syl words)
wordSort.hint: Try removing the suffix. Is the vowel short? Is it a single final consonant? For two-syllable words, where does the stress fall?
wordSort.answerNote: No doubling: entered, listened, helped, opened. Doubled: permitted, committed, bigger, thinner, occurred.
wordSort.exampleLine: enter → entered (stress on EN-, no double) | permit → permitted (stress on -MIT, double)

wordShed.sentence: It occurred to the detective that the footprints could only have been made after the rain.
wordShed.morphology: occur (v) → occurred (past) → occurring (pres part) → occurrence (n) → recur (v) → recurred (past)
